# Keep content in voice

Score and fix content against a voice profile with the local `kapi` CLI —
offline, no account. One loop: load the voice guide before writing, score a
draft, fix what drifts.

## Profiles

A profile comes from any of: a built-in pack (`--pack`), a git-shareable
YAML (`--profile-file`), or the local store (`--profile`). List options with
`kapi voice profiles`. Packs: `professional-b2b`, `friendly-dtc`,
`technical-docs`, `marketing-blog`, `customer-support`.

**Inside a project, the profile is part of the context — don't pass a flag.** When
the project binds a voice profile (a `defaults.voice` recipe entry, or a
`.kapi/voice.yaml` — or a `voice.yaml` at the project root), run `kapi voice check
<file>` and `kapi voice guide` with **no**
`--profile`/`--profile-file`/`--pack` — kapi resolves the project's voice. Pass a
flag only for a one-off outside a project, or to override the bound profile. See
[project.md](project.md).

# Edit content in any format

Edit the text inside a file an editor can't open directly — a Word document, a
PowerPoint deck, a JSON catalog, an XLIFF file, Markdown — and write it back in
the same format, byte-for-byte except for the text you changed. You do the
editing; kapi parses the format, enforces a faithful round-trip, and is the
checker. No model provider is involved.

This is the **read → edit → write → verify** loop. It is the deliberate,
reviewed counterpart to a `ksed` find-and-replace (see [toolbox.md](toolbox.md)):
reach for this loop when you are rewriting block text by hand (an on-brand fix, a
clarity pass, a terminology correction), and for `ksed` when a regex
substitution expresses the change.

## 1. Read the blocks

`kapi inspect` parses any format into one record per content block — the text,
the block's structural role, a stable `id`, and a `content_hash`:

```bash
kapi inspect report.docx --jsonl
```

events.text:
Fixed. README.md scores **100** against the Northwind profile, up from 85.

**What was off** — three major vocabulary findings, all forbidden terms:

| Term | Fix |
|---|---|
| `cutting-edge` | dropped (marketing superlative) |
| `utilize` | → `use` (preferred term) |
| `leverage` | → `use` |

```diff
-Northwind is a cutting-edge platform that lets teams utilize their content across every channel. Leverage our workspace to ship faster.
+Northwind is a platform that lets you use your content across every channel. Use our workspace to ship faster.
```

One judgment call beyond the flagged terms: I switched `teams` → `you`. The profile sets `person_pov: second` and says "Address the reader as you," but the rule-based style check scored 100 either way, so it didn't flag — revert that clause if you meant the third-person framing.

Notes on how this ran:

- No `.kapi` project here (`kapi status` found none), so I treated it as a one-off and passed `--profile-file voice.yaml`. If README checking becomes recurring, binding a project would let `kapi voice check` and `kapi check --ship` resolve the profile with no flags.
- The edit went through `kapi inspect` → `kapi apply` (previewed with `--diff` first), not a text overwrite, so the Markdown structure round-tripped intact.
- This isn't a git repo, so there's no undo for the overwrite beyond the diff above.

Since `utilize`/`leverage` are already rules in `voice.yaml`, there's nothing to add at the source — the profile caught these correctly.

events.text:
Fixed. New `README.md`:

```markdown
# Northwind

Northwind lets you use your content across every channel. Work from one workspace and ship faster.
```

What changed:

- **All three forbidden terms removed** — "cutting-edge", "utilize", and "Leverage" are gone; "use" (the profile's preferred term) replaces the last two. Verified with a grep scan.
- **Second person** — "lets teams utilize their content" → "lets you use your content"; "our workspace" → "one workspace", so nothing speaks from the company's side.
- **Superlative dropped** — "is a cutting-edge platform that" collapses to "lets", which also shortens the sentence and keeps it active.

I kept "ship faster" from the original. It's a comparative rather than a superlative, so it doesn't trip the marketing rule, and dropping it would have removed a claim you presumably want to make. Say the word if you'd rather it go too.

One judgment call worth flagging: I stayed close to the original's claims rather than expanding the README. A plainer voice tends to leave room for a concrete sentence about what the workspace actually does — but inventing that would be writing new copy, not a voice fix.
